newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia may overturn voluntary euthanasia law.
newsitem.headline: Australia may overturn voluntary euthanasia law.

text.p: The world's first voluntary euthanasia law is set to face another, and possibly its toughest, challenge when the Australian parliament on Monday debates a private-members bill aimed at overturning the law.

Many pro-euthanasia supporters openly admit the bill will probably pass in a conscience vote by parliamentarians, with both the Prime Minister John Howard and Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley publicly opposing euthanasia.
"Certainly talking to senior ministers I am disappointed," said Northern Territory Attorney General Denis Burke.
"It would appear that from the confident points of view I'm getting, the numbers are there...to support the bill and I think that in itself is a shame," Burke told reporters on Sunday.

The Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law, which came into effect in July, was used for the first time on September 22 when former carpenter Bob Dent, who was suffering terminal cancer, took his life with a lethal injection.
The law allows terminally-ill patients to end their life by lethal injection or pill as long as they meet strict conditions.
Under the Australian constitution, the national parliament can overturn territorial law, but not state law.

"If the Commonwealth (of Australia) wants to moralise, do what we did -- address the issue of euthanasia, debate it honestly and courageously. But don't try to use a mechanism to attack one territory which has had the courage to address this issue," said Burke.
Pro and anti-euthanasia supporters on Sunday gathered forces in a bid to influence the debate, with both the Anglican and Catholic Churches strongly urging the law be overturned.
The Standing Committee of the Anglican General Synod, the church's peak policy body in Australia, called for the the law to be "struck down because it permits intentional killing".
Anglican Reverend Bruce Kaye said in a statement the motion should not be seen as a direction to Anglican MPs but "certainly as a strong recommendation".

"We believe there is considerable confusion...between the use of the term 'euthanasia' to describe the intentional killing of a fellow human being; and its use to describe the cessation of futile treatment that results in unnecessary prolongation of life and suffering," Kaye said.
"It's the former to which we are opposed, and we therefore believe the Northern Territory legislation would be struck down because it permits intentional killing," he said.

Catholic Church leaders in South Australia state on Sunday released a letter written to the state's 12 lower house national parliamentarians urging the law be overturned, saying terminally ill patients can best be cared for by extending palliative care.
"We believe that it is essential that the federal parliament does exercise its right and responsibility to act as a house of review of legislation in the territories," the letter said.

In contrast, Northern Territory politicans on Sunday rallied at Canberra's parliament house to issue a petition to parliament against the anti-euthanasia bill. The petition argues the bill, if passed, would diminish the Territory's self-governing powers.
The Northern Territory's Chief Minister Shane Stone offered to restrict the euthanasia law to residents of the territory in an attempt top salvage the law.
"One of the great arguments being used against us is that we have legislated for the whole of Australia," Stone said.
"If that is the sticking point, if the legislation is amended so that you have to be a Territorian to access it, then does that resolve the problem?"
Stone said he would also ask the prime minister to defer the debate on the anti-euthanasia bill until the outcome of a challenge to the law before the High Court on November 15.
